passage: Diwali lamps lined the balcony of the Chembur flat when a man left a parcel at the door and hurried off. Nazia, five, peeped at him through the grille. Later Santosh Mama crouched beside her. "Did the man have a red cap on?" Nazia thought, then nodded. That night she told Ammi, "The parcel man had a big red cap, like a fire engine!" Ammi, who had signed for the parcel, tilted her head. The man had been bare-headed, his hair oiled flat. Nazia's eyes stayed sure.

qa.q: What did Santosh Mama ask Nazia?
qa.a: He asked, "Did the man have a red cap on?"

qa.q: How sure does Nazia seem about the red cap, and what does that suggest?
qa.a: She seems excited and completely sure, even though the man was bare-headed; the words of the question have become part of what she believes she saw.

qa.q: How could Santosh Mama have asked so that Nazia's own memory stayed clearer?
qa.a: He could ask an open question such as "What did the man look like?" and let her answer without any hints.

qa.q: What is it like for Ammi when Nazia describes the red cap?
qa.a: Ammi is puzzled, because she saw the man had no cap; she may guess the idea came from a question rather than from Nazia's own eyes.

grounding: Shows an adult's question about a red cap seeding a detail the young child later remembers as real.

passage: It was the Dasara holidays, Irfan, and the Mysore palace was lit with thousands of bulbs. Everyone in my family swears little Kavitha saw the monkey. I was nine. My brother Ravi has told it at every wedding since: the monkey snatched my banana, I screamed, Appa chased it round a pillar. I can see it clearly, the grey fur, the glowing bulbs, my own shriek. Then last year, clearing a trunk, I found Amma's letter from that trip. It says I slept in the bus the whole evening, and it was Ravi's banana. Now I honestly cannot tell which pictures are mine and which I borrowed from all that retelling.

qa.q: During which holidays did the family visit the palace?
qa.a: It was the Dasara holidays, when the palace was lit with thousands of bulbs.

qa.q: How does Kavitha feel after reading Amma's old letter?
qa.a: Kavitha feels unsettled and confused, because the pictures of the monkey still feel vivid and real, yet the letter says Kavitha slept in the bus the whole evening.

qa.q: At the point when Ravi began retelling the story at weddings, what could the family have done differently?
qa.a: Someone could have asked young Kavitha what was actually seen before telling it for Kavitha, or checked Amma's letter, so the family version did not replace the child's own.

qa.q: How might Ravi see the story now that the letter says it was his banana?
qa.a: Ravi might be surprised or sheepish, since Ravi told it at every wedding with Kavitha screaming; Ravi's own retelling shaped the memory too.

grounding: Illustrates a child's trip memory blending with family retellings until the narrator cannot tell what was seen from what was told.

subtype: Witnessing an event and then reading reports [Actor]
passage:
Holi, 9:40 pm. Still pink behind my ears.
Around four, near the college gate, a scooter clipped an auto. I was on the steps, half blind with gulal, and heard the crunch more than saw it. Nobody was hurt, just a bent mirror and a lot of shouting.
Tonight the colony group is full of it. Someone posted a local news clip saying the scooter guy was racing and on his phone. Nazia texted, "Gautam, you were right there, was he on the phone?" And yes. I can see it now, the phone pressed to his ear, the speed. I wrote back, "100%, he was."
Funny, I didn't mention a phone to anyone this afternoon. But I'm sure. Totally sure.

qa.q: What did Gautam text back to Nazia?
qa.a: Gautam wrote back, "100%, he was."

qa.q: How confident does Gautam feel about the phone, and what in the entry hints that this confidence may be misplaced?
qa.a: Gautam feels totally sure, yet admits being half blind with gulal, hearing the crunch more than seeing it, and not mentioning a phone to anyone that afternoon.

qa.q: What could Gautam do before posting "100%" in the group?
qa.a: Gautam could write down only what was seen and heard at four, keep it apart from the news clip and the chat, and reply honestly, "I'm not sure about a phone."

qa.q: How might the scooter rider be affected if the colony group believes Gautam?
qa.a: The rider could be blamed for using a phone on the word of a confident eyewitness who may never have seen one, which would feel deeply unfair if it was not true.

grounding: Shows a witness absorbing a phone detail from a news clip and group chat and feeling fully certain about it.

subtype: Asking open questions and noting memory early [Observer]
passage:
Vidya had been teaching at the primary school for three weeks when Tenzin came in from recess with a torn sleeve and a red face. Vidya was about to ask, "Did Kunal pull your shirt?" when Sonali, the Class 2 coordinator, knelt first.
"Tenzin, tell me what happened."
He sniffed. "We were on the slide. Someone tugged. It ripped."
"Then what?"
"I fell on the sand."
Sonali didn't mention Kunal once. She wrote Tenzin's words on a slip, added the time, 11:20, and read them back to him. He nodded. Vidya noticed her own question still sitting on her tongue, already carrying a name the boy had never said.

qa.q: What time did Sonali write on the slip?
qa.a: She added the time, 11:20.

qa.q: What might Vidya be feeling on noticing the question still sitting on her tongue?
qa.a: She likely feels a jolt of embarrassment mixed with relief, seeing that her question would have put Kunal's name into Tenzin's account.

qa.q: Which of Sonali's steps keeps Tenzin's account his own, and why?
qa.a: She asks "tell me what happened" and "then what?" without naming anyone, and writes his words down straight away, before later talk can reshape them.

qa.q: What would change if Vidya had asked about Kunal first?
qa.a: Tenzin might have agreed that Kunal pulled his shirt and later remembered it that way, and Kunal could be blamed for a tug nobody saw.

grounding: An observer watches a coordinator gather a child's account with an open question and write it down at once.

passage: I sit between Ishita and Manjula at the design studio, so I heard all of it on Monday. Manjula said Ishita had promised to send the tile samples to the client by Friday. Ishita's jaw tightened, and I braced for a fight. Instead she said, slowly, "This is how I remember it: you'd send them and I'd do the drawings. But I could be wrong." She scrolled back through their team chat, lips moving. Then she stopped and turned the screen toward Manjula. There it was, Thursday, her own message: "I'll courier the samples tomorrow." Ishita let out a short laugh, said, "Okay, that one's on me," and booked a pickup before lunch. Manjula's shoulders dropped. I can't say what Ishita felt, but she didn't argue again.

qa.q: Where did Ishita look to check what had been agreed?
qa.a: She scrolled back through their team chat.

qa.q: What does Ishita's short laugh after seeing the message suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: It suggests a flash of embarrassment mixed with relief that the question was settled, since she owns the mistake and books the pickup straight away.

qa.q: Which choice kept the disagreement from turning into a fight, and why?
qa.a: Saying "this is how I remember it" and checking the chat; it left room to be wrong and let the message decide, instead of two confident memories clashing.

qa.q: How might Manjula see Ishita after this?
qa.a: Manjula likely feels relieved and respected, and may trust Ishita more, because Ishita checked the facts and admitted the slip instead of insisting.

grounding: An observer describes an adult framing a dispute as her own memory and checking the chat before deciding who was right.

passage:
The paper boats for Kartik Purnima were drying on the verandah when the panchayat van rolled through the village near Puri, its loudspeaker crackling: a cyclone warning, move to the school shelter by evening. Pooja, lying on the charpai with her phone, didn't look up.
"Pooja, Maa says pack your books," her cousin Pranav called, already untying the goats.
"Every year they shout this," she said, thumbing past a dance clip. "Remember last Kartik? Two drops of rain."
Outside, the sky over the casuarina trees had turned the colour of wet cement, and the palms were bending. Pooja pulled her dupatta over her feet and kept scrolling. Nothing had ever happened here. Why would it now?

qa.q: What did the loudspeaker announce?
qa.a: A cyclone warning, telling people to move to the school shelter by evening.

qa.q: Why does Pooja keep scrolling, and how does she seem to feel?
qa.a: She feels calm and a little bored, because past warnings brought only "two drops of rain", so she assumes nothing will happen this time either.

qa.q: What small step could Pooja take right now, even if she doubts the warning?
qa.a: She could pack her books and go with the family to the school shelter; if the cyclone misses, she has lost only one evening.

qa.q: How might Pranav feel watching Pooja stay on the charpai?
qa.a: Pranav may feel worried and frustrated, busy with the goats while Pooja ignores both the warning and the darkening sky.

grounding: A teenager shrugs off a cyclone warning because past warnings came to nothing, and keeps scrolling.

passage: It was Christmas week, Rekha, the crib half-built in the front room, when the church bell began ringing out of turn. The river had been rising for two days. Everyone in our lane still teases me: "Elizabeth, the girl who saved her certificates and lost her shoes." I was twenty. The panchayat man shouted for us to leave for the high school. Appachan said, "It always comes to the steps and stops," and began wrapping the brass lamps in newspaper. I sat folding my college papers into plastic, calm as anything. Within an hour the water was at our knees inside the house. We waded out holding hands, the crib floating behind us. I still dream about that one wasted hour.

qa.q: What did Appachan say about the river?
qa.a: Appachan said, "It always comes to the steps and stops."

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel while folding the college papers, and what does the story show about that feeling?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt calm, sure the river would stop as usual, and that calm cost the family an hour, which is why the memory still returns in dreams.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what could the family have chosen instead?
qa.a: When the panchayat man told them to leave, they chose to pack; walking out at once with only papers would have got them to the high school before the water came in.

qa.q: How might Appachan have felt as the water reached their knees inside the house?
qa.a: Appachan likely felt shocked and frightened, and perhaps guilty, since the belief that the river always stops at the steps kept the family inside.

grounding: An elder recalls her family pausing to pack under a real flood warning, sure the river would stop as it usually did.

subtype: Colleagues stay put when the alarm rings [Observer]
passage:
Shreya: fire alarm going off on our floor 😬
Aadhya: are you out??
Shreya: no one's moving. everyone's just typing
Shreya: the guy from accounts looked at the intern, the intern looked at the manager, and the manager is still on his call
Aadhya: probably a drill but GO
Shreya: I know I know. feels so weird to be the only one standing up
Aadhya: weird is fine. smoke is not
Shreya: ok taking my bag and heading to the stairs
Shreya: wait the whole row just got up behind me
Shreya: they were all waiting for somebody to go first 😅
Aadhya: see? told you
Shreya: on the stairs now. smells like burnt toast from the pantry

qa.q: What was the manager doing when the alarm rang?
qa.a: The manager was still on his call.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling before taking the bag?
qa.a: Shreya felt awkward and self-conscious about being the only one standing up, while also sensing that leaving was the right thing.

qa.q: What would you advise someone who notices coworkers ignoring an alarm?
qa.a: Get up and leave calmly without waiting; as Shreya found, one person moving often gives everyone else permission to follow.

qa.q: Why might the rest of the row have waited to stand up?
qa.a: Each person was watching the others for a cue, and seeing nobody move made staying seem normal, so they likely felt relieved once someone went first.

grounding: An employee sees coworkers keep working through a fire alarm until one person stands, and then the whole row follows.

passage:
The official alert buzzed at 10:40 p.m.: heavy rain, low-lying streets may flood, move to higher floors. Zeenat's phone was on eleven percent and the power had just gone. Her flatmate Jyoti was stuck at her office across the city.
Zeenat didn't wait to see water at the door. She pulled out the small bag she kept under her bed: torch, copies of her papers, a charger, biscuits, a water bottle. She texted Jyoti, "Going up to Mrs. Pillai on the third floor. Your laptop is with me." She had walked the back staircase the week she moved in, so she climbed it in the dark without fumbling.
The landlord chuckled on the landing. "Madam, this street never floods."
By morning the water had only reached the gate. Zeenat felt a bit silly carrying her bag back down, but she was smiling.

qa.q: What was in the bag Zeenat kept under the bed?
qa.a: A torch, copies of her papers, a charger, biscuits and a water bottle.

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel carrying the bag back down in the morning?
qa.a: She felt a bit silly, but she was smiling, content that a small embarrassment was better than being caught by rising water.

qa.q: Which of Zeenat's habits helped most when the alert came late at night?
qa.a: Keeping a packed bag and knowing the back staircase let her act in the dark, on a low phone, without waiting for proof.

qa.q: What was it like for Jyoti, stuck across the city, to get Zeenat's text?
qa.a: Jyoti probably felt relieved to know where Zeenat was and that the laptop was safe, instead of worrying all night.

grounding: An adult follows an official flood alert at night with a ready bag and a known exit, accepting the mild embarrassment of a false alarm.

passage:
The power went out on Christmas Eve just as the carol group reached the end of the lane, and someone had to fetch candles from Francis's house, past the old well.
"Not me," Francis said, gripping the gate. "The white lady sits on that well after dark. Everybody knows."
Vandana, holding the matchbox, asked, "Who actually saw her?"
Francis opened his mouth. Vandana herself had told him in Class 2. The big boys said it every monsoon. Even the bakery aunty joked about it. He had heard it a hundred times, so it felt as solid as the well itself.
But nobody, he realised, had ever said, "I saw her."
Still, his feet did not move. The carols waited in the dark.

qa.q: Where did someone have to go to fetch candles?
qa.a: To Francis's house, past the old well.

qa.q: Why does the story about the white lady feel true to Francis?
qa.a: He has heard it so many times, from Vandana, the big boys and the bakery aunty, that it feels familiar and solid, so he stays scared even though nobody ever saw her.

qa.q: What small step could help Francis test the story?
qa.a: He could ask each person where they heard it, notice that no one says "I saw her", and then walk to the well with Vandana and a torch.

qa.q: How might Vandana feel when Francis repeats a story she once told him?
qa.a: She may feel a bit guilty or amused, realising her Class 2 tale has become something Francis now treats as fact.

grounding: Shows a child believing a ghost story because it has been repeated so often that it feels familiar and therefore true.
